newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-European central bank monetary policy-by Olaf Liedtke.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-European central bank monetary policy-by Olaf Liedtke.

text.p: By Dr Olaf Liedtke, international financial market economist at Landesbank Hessen-Thueringen in Frankfurt

The European Central Bank (ECB) will adopt neither the money supply targeting practised by the Bundesbank, nor the direct inflation control pursued by the Bank of England. This is the quintessence of statements made by the European Monetary Institute (EMI) on the monetary strategy for the single currency.

The exact definition of this "third way" will be up to the central bank council of the ECB. Nevertheless, a preliminary decision has been taken in as much as some control concepts such as an exchange rate target, interest rate control and the management of the nominal gross national product were classified as inadequate.

The EMI has thus created a framework for monetary strategy which in general corresponds to the principles of efficiency, calculability and transparency, which is guided by medium-term requirements and which shows a certain continuity with regard to the former monetary strategies in Europe. This should strengthen confidence in the stability of the value of the Euro.

Even though the EMI has not decided between inflation and money supply management, the signs that the ECB will at first conduct something like inflation management are on the increase - a pragmatic decision. In fact, the two strategies are more similar in their practical realisation than in their theoretical concepts; also, the often analysed fundamental monetary conditions in Germany cannot be translated to a newly created currency area in a ratio of one on one.

The central prerequisite for the money supply policy of the Bundesbank to achieve stability is mainly - even with short-term distortions in monetary developments - the stability of money demand over the medium term.

It ensures that, with given non-monetary conditions, monetary influences will have a predictable effect on the ultimate objective of monetary policy - the stability of the value of money over the medium term.

The comparison between the money supply target and actual monetary developments can yield information on the direction and the effects of monetary policy at an early stage only, when money demand is not subject to erratic fluctuations. This function of money supply growth as an indicator leads to a steadying of inflationary expectations, for instance among the parties to the collective wage negotiations and in social policy.

This is an advantage as compared to inflation management, where information an monetary developments are as a rule only available with a time-lag of six to eight quarters. This effect should not be underestimated. In addition, the announcement of an interim target means having to face continuing scrutiny by the markets.

Nobody is at present able to make any predictions on the stability of the connections between monetary policy, the development of the money supply and rates of inflation in the European monetary area. Deviations from the monetary target due to unstable money demand, could in general be evaluated by market participants as a credibility gap. In any case, they are not expected to accept it as calmly as in the case of German money supply management.

This makes it unnecessarily complicated for the ECB to achieve the necessary reputation in monetary policy matters - with adverse effects on capital market interest rates, the external value of the Euro and thus last but not least on the conditions for capital investments in the monetary union.
The preliminary waiver of a monetary target does not mean that the ECB might refrain from developing and observing suitable monetary aggregates tor the monetary union.

This could on the one hand facilitate the recognition of inflationary tendencies, on the other hand, a stable connection between the development of the money supply and the rate of inflation is expected to emerge in the longer run.

This indicates that monetary policy at the start of monetary union will be similar to a "trial and error" process where additional indicators are used for the evaluation of monetary impetus. True, this reduces the transparency of the monetary objectives and is likely to contain some surprises for the money and capital markets, but nevertheless, it might help the reputation of the ECB if it is ultimately successful in stabilising the purchasing power of the Euro.

Ensuring a low rate of inflation for the Euro is not easy, simply because we do not yet have a definition of "Euro inflation". It will be necessary to develop a basket of commodities as a basis for the cost-of-living index which on the one hand provides a representative model of the entire Euro currency area and on the other hand keeps in line with the national baskets of commodities. In no way may the official rate of inflation for the Euro deviate significantly from that which applies to individual countries or regions. The Euro would necessarily be discredited if the statistical data on Euro inflation deviated from the experience of the people made in their specific environment.

Summing up, it must be said that the markets will have to adapt to a pragmatic European monetary policy at the start of the single currency. This policy will be determined by a prudent but continuous adjustment of central bank interest rates in accordance with the principle "learning by doing".

Extraordinary developments of the money supply or an increased volatility of money market interest rates therefore should not be overestimated as indicators for the monetary orientation of the ECB. The professional "ECB watchers" should therefore be patient and avoid commenting too loudly during the first years of monetary union when assessing the monetary policy of the ECB.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of the Landesbank Hessen-Thueringen or of Reuters.)
